blocks.x: Hello Jazz fans, this is George Gayno, band Jewish and guitarist of New Orleans, Louisiana.
This is Bill Russell, interviewing George Gayno at 600 Charter Street, and the date is June the 10th, 1960. Okay, can you tell us where you were born and just the exact date?
Yes, Bill, I was born on the 25th day of May 1907 in the Creole downtown section of New Orleans.
Can you tell us about, did anyone in your family play? Your father, mother, anyone play any music?

Well, I had an uncle who used to play guitar, Emil Gayno. He used to play with a band with slow drag in it, maybe 50 or 60 years ago. They had a small band, and I mean they played a lot of Creole songs. I remember slow drag telling me one of the main numbers they used to have was a number called, Macaque Manger Piment.
Is that a respectable title?
Yeah, that'd be the monkey pepper chord or something like that. You can imagine the chords went with that.
Tell us about your first interest in music. When you were a little boy, did you start on any instrument?

Well, when I was a small boy, Bill, I became intrigued with a ukulele I saw in a small place on Orleans between Johnson and Preah called Miss Campanelle. And which incidentally, that place is still there right now. And I just sold papers and shined shoes and did everything I could to get that uke. And I didn't have it over two or three weeks with an instruction book that I could play it pretty well, just to entertain the gang on the street at night. But I never had in my mind that one day that would be the start of a musical career for me.
How old were you about when you got there?

Oh, I was about eleven or twelve. I was shining shoes around here and I got that ukulele. I played a, in other words, a convention came to town. And, of course, the ukulele didn't cost but two and a half, but trying to get two and a half them days was rough. And I went up there and shined shoes so my fingers was to the bone. But I finally got that two and a half and bought that ukulele.
Did you follow any parades in those days?

Oh, yeah. That's all we did, followed parades in them days. I mean, a strange thing, I used to hang on, follow one band more than ever. It was the Sam Morgan Jazz Band. And little did I realize then, a little old guy, eleven years old, running around the street, barefooted, that one day I was going to play in that band for six years.
Where were they playing those days?

Well, they were playing different places. I didn't go to the places they played, but I used to meet them on Sunday advertising. Oh, in the wagon. Advertising on the street, not hop on and give me a bunch of folders, or circulars in other words they call them. I would deliver them just to be out there with them, you know. Something like that hand bill of Kid Thomas? That's right, a hand bill. That's really what it was, a hand bill.
Can you tell us anything else about your family? Did your father favor you?

Oh no, no indeed. No indeed, man, no indeed. You see, my father was a plasterer. And my uncle was a bricklayer, and my grandfather was a plasterer. And it was just the customs of the Creoles that nobody was supposed to break away from nothing. If he was a plasterer, then I was supposed to be a plasterer. Well, when I got to be around 16 years old, they took me, him and Sam Augustin, which was Johnny St. Cyr's stepfather. I went to work with them as a plasterer's apprentice, getting $1.60 a day. That's what it was. And I mean, it was a grind. It was really rough. Ain't no hours. Just wait till he said get through. So, I mean, I just kept on that, and I mean, that was beginning to get the best of me, and I mean, the work was really hard. And I went out to dance one night with my cousin Margaret and I heard, John Marrera play a banjo, and that was it. He couldn't have got me up with a 10-foot pull to 45 from there, or I'd have made up my mind I was going to play a banjo.
Tell us about your first job when you started in the...

Well, I mean, as I say, I was working and working, and I mean, it looked like I was just the unhappiest guy in town. And one day a friend of mine come off a show. He was a youngster like myself. Him and I were good friends. And incidentally, he's the guy that is the cause of me being a musician today. Gilbert Young, a trumpet player. I mean, he came to town. He came to see me, and he asked me would I come out with him that night. He wanted to go to a place to see some fellow around some business, so he brought me to a place called the Humminbird Cabaret. Well, I had never been in a cabaret in my life before. All I did was went to church and stayed around home, and the cabaret, if they'd have thought I went in a cabaret, they'd allow me to scalp me like an Indian, you know?
Were you raised as a Catholic?
Oh, yeah, yeah. I was an altar boy at St. Catherine Church.
Over there on Tulane?

I was on Tulane across from the charity hospital. Yeah, I was baptized and confirmed by Father Cuddy. Uh-huh. And so, well, anyhow, Gilbert took me out in this place. It was in the year 1927 on the St. Joseph night. And I walked in there, and I had never seen nothing like that. They had a group in there called the Baby Dolls. They had a stocking full of $100 bills, and I was a perfect square. I never saw nothing like that in my life. And I just added up. And from that night on, I ain't never went back home.
What kind of a band was that?

Well, there was a five-piece band. There was a band that was Kid Clayton on trumpet, George Williams on drum, Tink Batiste on piano, Pete Beatty playing saxophone, and Earl Stockmeyer playing banjo. So after I went there that first night and I saw that, to me, that was a new world. I felt like somebody who got rejuvenated all over again. I knew that was the life for me, that and no other life. So I began to hang in the place every night. I practically lived in it. So I got to become friends with the band. I'd bring them drinks when I'd be at the table. And Earl Stockmeyer and I got to be good friends. So when I took his banjo and I couldn't play a tenor the way a banjo should be played, but I kept fooling with it and I tuned it like I had tuned my uke. I could play that uke very well. I didn't know I could play in the band with it like that. They wasn't playing but in two keys all night, no how, B flat and F. So finally I got to know that I could play my uke. with what they were playing. And that's all I wanted to know. From that I was more understanding than Earl was. So what happens is he, about, that went on for about five or six months and one night he got very sick. And he didn't come back in the wake and about two or three weeks he died. So Professor Cook put me in the band. Says I want Creole George to stay in the band. Professor Cook was the guy who owned the joint. Him and his wife Evelyn, there was one of the finest dance teams in the city. Why did they call him Professor? Well that's what you, well you know he was just a guy was all full of flesh, always a tuxedo and a whistle in his mouth. Oh he had a big mind, you know, but he had a wonderful dance team. But he was in charge of it. And all them guys used to come around and say, Well man, you could have given the job to this banjo player and that banjo player. He said, I'm going to give it to him. He said, because I got faith in him that in six months he's going to cut everybody in town. I said, well I'm going to try to live up to it as much as I could. So I mean I was just playing, I wasn't getting nowhere, but to go back like I told you I met my cousin Margaret. And she asked me to take her to a dance one night and I heard John Moreira play. That was the banjo master. I never heard nobody in my life play no banjo like that. That was the, oh that, that, that, that, that. Words will never express how well this man could play.

But Lawrence isn't here to talk about him anymore. And you're one of the few people that really could describe. Did he play mostly the chord style? Just say four beats to a major. Did he put in extra beats?

Oh no, yeah, yeah, yeah, he was a wonderful chord man, but you see the question of it is he stuck close to the orchestration. In other words, he told me this when I went to take lessons for him. He said, George, no matter where you go, if you go play with a guy tonight, and this guy's got a piece of music that you don't have, copy the chords down so you go home and you'll memorize the chords that's on the orchestration. Because they're only true chords, and these are the kind of chords you must stay by. Only depend on your ear when there's no music around. He says, but when you can take a finer part, you can write those chords off and make sure you take those chords. And play them chords all the time, he says, and you'll find out that's where the real beauty of it lies. Because all arrangers know what they're doing. You see, they was getting away from strictly the ear music then. Stock numbers was coming in. And a guy had to sit down and do something with a part if he just couldn't master it to do something with it. You know what I mean? It was one of them thing.
Did he ever take many solos or one-string solos?

Well, no. You see, that's where I was better than he was. You see, that's what made me, as I say, I'm better than my teacher. As far as that goes. You see, my banjo playing today, that's what makes me stand out as a banjo player. It isn't that I make more chords than the other fella, or I read more better than him. I can solo more better than him. You see, I take all single-string solos. We'll say like Charlie Christian or somebody like that. And you get the beauty about taking all them broken-off pegs of yours and break them. And all such things as that. I mean, that's where when a man said take one, well, I mean, today you go. That possibly where some may differ and say it don't belong in the music, I'll agree to that, too. But today it's a demand. You take right now, I think one of the finest chord men in the business is Johnny St. Cyr. But he can't get a job because he cares solo. There isn't anything wrong with Johnny. I think Johnny's a fine musician and as great a chord man as they got anywhere in the country. But he cares solo. And today, if you don't take one, you ain't got no job. So you see, that was an issue that was forced upon you. Take one. Play the flute part. Play the heavy part. As long as you're able to take one. So that's why I had to change my style all around. And get away practically from too much rhythm and begin to be a solo banjo player. That's it.
Anything else about John Marrero's style? What kind of a banjo did he use?
Well, he used the standard vega them days. You see, the vega was...
Did he have a resonator in those days?

Oh, yes, it had a resonator. It had a resonator and an armrest and a head guard. Most of you see plenty of banjos today. The guy don't have no head guard on them. But that little piece covered the head. You know, when you hit with the pick that kept the head from getting black or something like that.

By the way, Lawrence showed me his banjo a couple years ago. He had a mute on it, too. I forget how Lawrence is... Yeah. Some sort of a mute. Yeah. Somebody else has one. McLean. I think you use your knee or push something.
Oh, yeah.
Lawrence is a different type. Oh, yeah.

You see, some screw on the back of the bridge. Some screw is right on the string and you pull it right to the bridge. And they give it a muted sound. That's what Lawrence said. But there was a banjo that came out called a silver bell bacon.
Oh, yeah.
And that bacon had what you call some kind of a... Well, it was a... It was a mute, but it was...
A lever or something.

Yeah, a lever. That's right. It was a lever that was worked by the leg. When it was down, you had a clear tone. When you wanted the muted sound, you brought up your leg and squeezed the lever against the banjo. That's what it was.
John Marrero just had an ordinary...

Oh, he had an ordinary vega. Just an ordinary vega. But the guy could play. Oh, he could play. You see, he played with taste and class and finesse. And everybody in town wanted him. And that's what it is, you see. And I went to him and I took lessons with him for about seven months. And when he turned me loose, he said, There ain't anything no more I can show you.
How much did he charge you?
Fifty cents. But I was rugged getting that fifty cents, I tell you.
How often a week did you go?
I took three lessons a week.
Three?
Oh, yeah. I took three.
So how long did he teach you each day?

Well, I'd say for about four to five minutes. Well, you see, this is the thing, too. He liked me. And that is the main issue that I wanted to talk about concerning this teaching proposition. You see, it isn't the music a teacher knows or how much great abilities he has as a teacher. It's how well he's able to transmit that which is within him into his student. That's what makes a great teacher from my viewpoint. Men come to my house, boys or whatever it is, whether they're white, colored, Mexican, Indian. Everybody leaves my house after seven months and they can play. Anybody leaves my house to stay with me a while, they can play. Because that is the secret of my teaching. I don't ever advertise how great a musician I am, how great a banjo player I am. Let the other fellas say that. But one thing I do know, that I have a tendency within me that I'm able to transmit that which is in me to my student. And that, I say, is the secret of a good teacher.
In regard to John, I keep pumping you about John Marrero. Oh, he's way pumping about, I tell you.
He's way pumping about.
Hardly any of the Marrero's left to talk for themselves. So, did he use a method, any kind of a book?
Yeah, Arthur Black. Arthur Black Methods. That's the first method he got me to teach you.
Did you have any other music? Did he write out pieces for you?

Oh, yeah. Well, yeah. Well, you see, everything I do today is practically what he done for me. You see, because I've been having a few students coming to me from different schools around here. You tell them make C, they make the note of C. You see, make A, they make the note of A. Whoever is teaching them is going about the wrong way. Now, if you had a violin pupil, that would be right. Because a violin is a note instrument. But the banjo is a chord instrument. So, what you want to learn a man to do, you want to learn him how to count one, two, three, four beats to the measure. You want to learn him how to make the chord of A7. Or the chord of D minor. Not the note of D. Or the chord of F. And that's the whole trouble. I don't know how they're teaching them. But, I mean, if that's their way, they would spend... Well, in fact, I got a boy right now, Ivory Foster. He's been taking lessons nine months out here from some teacher. And he come in the house and he can't make the chord of C. I mean, that's just one of them things. I mean, you know, in other words... Well, I mean, a lot of my... That's a very good friend of mine. No name called. I told him, I said... Man, I said, you got a guy. I said, you a saxophone player. I said, and you teaching so-and-so guitar. I said, and every time I look, you watching my fingers to see what chord I'm making. So you go back and show that to somebody else. I said, man, I don't think you're going to make the greatest of guitar teacher. He said, well, my conception is, man, I don't care if the cat learned or not. All I want is the $2. Well, you see, with me, it ain't like that. If a guy come to me and he can't learn something in two weeks, I said, look, man, I'll come back.

Here's something I want you to... Even if I have to interrupt your train of thought. There was one nice little thing you told me about once when you worked with Albert Glenny. He told you that pick out a good man to watch and then ask him questions and things like that. Do you remember? What was that he said to you once? Something about... Well, yeah, well... What was some advice he gave you?

Well, the older men had all kind of things. I mean, I don't so well remember that answer. But one thing he did tell me... We were talking about chords one night, you see. And he says, this is one thing about music. He said, D minor might be the right chord. It might be the right chord. He says, but if everybody in the band would make A7, we'll say. But they make it together, then it's the right chord. He says, but where it becomes a bad chord is if two is making D minor and the other fellow is making A7. Then you got a conflict in music. He says, but you go... If they all make B flat and they make it together, that's the right chord. Well, I mean, he had a point there, you see. Because music in itself, in its effect, is the harmony that's balanced against the notes. I mean, if everybody make B flat, it's a perfect chord. But if this fellow make B and the other fellow make G and E make A, well, you got a perfect disc chord there, you know. One of those kind of things.

There's another thing I remember you've talked about, which we never did get on tape, that you're not ashamed to ask people questions to show you something. Whereas some musicians will try to act like they know it all already, and they're ashamed, you know, to ask somebody to show them anything. But you say, in the old days, you'd get together and you'd watch somebody and show me how to do that.

Well, you see, Bill, those days, that was the basic conception of music. Because you take all the great players around you, let's put it to that. Because, in fact, there was no such a thing as a great New Orleans musician. There was no such a thing. Some guys knew music. Some guys could read pretty well. But you couldn't put them in the class of a master musician. They were master players. In other words, they're dependent on learning the basic fundamentals of their instrument first. Know your instrument. That was the theme of the old man. Know your instrument. In other words, the music is good in its place. We can fight with that. We can wrestle with the music, play it, spell it. But once we get it in our head, how it go, the power we put behind it is the thing that's going to count. And the older man always was like that. You see, today, a guy figures that it makes him inferior to come to you and ask you what chord. He would rather sit down all night and make the wrong chord. But here's a good one like that. You take Manuel Sales, Danny Barker, myself, Poissy Sevier, Hendrick Kimball. All them men I'm telling you about were all good banjo players. And all of us got a knowledge of learning from each other. Say, man, what chord that was. Let me see how you done that. Or so and so. Well, look, I was playing the number last night and went to the bridge. What chord was in the bridge? E-7 or A minor. Well, that's it. Okay, man. But that way you knew. And you were going to go sit in a man's band. You wasn't going to cut no hog. But the other, the guy today, he just figured if he asks you, that makes you know, it's something to be ashamed of. That's why around your ring, you only got nobody left to play.
If I remember rightly now, it's coming to me a little bit. It seems like you said once, Glennie said, if you're going to ask somebody, don't ask a damn fool the question. Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Always. No, that's what he said. He said, every man can be taught something by somebody. But just so the man is not a damn fool. That's all. He said, make sure when you go to a man to ask him concerning something that the man is able to tell you what to do. And he's right. You understand? That's right. In other words, if I wanted to know something on the banjo, I'd ask people like Kimball and Sales. You understand what I mean? I wouldn't ask Black Walter because he wouldn't know. He's my friend and all, but he just don't know. You know what I mean? He's just sitting up there playing all night. But ask him, make G7. He don't know what G7 is at all. He just played by what he hear in his ear. But you could ask people like Sales and Kimball, anything, and they was able to ask it musically. You know, they were good musicians.
Yes, very good. All right, let's see. Can you tell us a little bit more about your first days? How long did you stay there at the Hummingbird, and where did you go after that?

Well, I stood at the Hummingbird for about, I'll say, about nine months. And one night, John had some misunderstanding in the band, and to my surprise, Papa Salistad called me in the band. I was just that good. My name had began to spread, you see, because the cabaret used to open at night. But in the daytime, they had plenty of advertisement, plenty of jobs at Millenburg, all that in the day. So I was gigging with Rene, Buddy Petit, Chris, and all them outside, and my name began to spread. That guy plays a good banjo. He's a good banjo player, you know. Chris Kelly, I remember him. Tell me I was the greatest banjo player in the world. Play on the job all day. Give me 50 cents. You're going to make it. You're going to make it. I said, and that's just, he just bullshitted me with that. But God knows I love, but I was going to make it, you know. Well, I mean, thank God. I finally did make it, too. You know what I mean? So I went to work with Salistad, and I stood with him, say, about a year. And one day I was sitting at home. We was living at 627 North Johnson. We're between St. Pete and Old Basin now, which is a part of the housing project. All that's gone now. And a big fella come to the door, all dressed up in the tuxi, knock at the door, and ask mama for me. And I come to the door, he says, are you George? I said, yes. He said, well, I'm Sam Morgan. Man, Sam Morgan, that sounded like Duke Ellington to me, you know, because them cats was really insane then. And they was playing in all the hotels and all the cool. And what I wanted to do, I was satisfied with Salistad, but Salistad wasn't doing plenty traveling. And a guy told me he was going to Mobile. That looked like he was going to Hindustan or somewhere. I'd never been across the street in my life, you see. So when he said we're going to play Mobile and all that, man, that sounded like going to New York or something. So he asked me, did I want to go on the road with him? So I said, yeah, I'll go on the road with you. So I went on the road, and I ate that dust out there. And, man, I went through all the hardships they had out there with him. And that leads to another question. You see, Johnny Dave was that regular banjo player. So I went on the road. You didn't tell me nothing about Johnny Dave. So I'd have net up all that dust and everything out there, and I'm getting better and better, though. I'm getting so that I'm able to take all them pretty one-string solos and all them kind of things. So we're going to play a job. Sam's got a job playing on the Temple Roof Garden. I'm me. I come on to the job. All I found out the job was going to be, say, Monday or Tuesday. I come up there all dressed up. When I got up there, Mr. Johnny Dave was standing there. He looked at me and said, well, that's all right, boy. I'm taking over tonight, and you know me. You know me. I've been that way ever since I was 12 years old. Who's taking over tonight, you know? So I look at him, and they say, yeah, Johnny's going to play. I say, well, okay, man. I said, Johnny's going to play. I took him down the corner, and I come home. Laid across the bed, barely crying like a baby. You know what I mean? Yeah, all because the roof garden was the big thing them days, all them pretty girls and everything up there. And I can play. I know I can play, and I want to play for them, but I'm denied that right. So I didn't say nothing. I went home. About three days after, yeah, he come knock on the door. So we're going to pass Chris Dan or something. I say, you're going to pass Chris Dan, not me. I say, man, don't never come here and ask me to play with y'all no more. I say, man, of all the things. I say, who do he think he is? I say, I play more with one hand tied behind my back than he ever could play with all that big talk he got. So I say, now y'all going to have to make a choice. Either it's going to be Johnny Dave playing banjo with you, or I'm going to play. I say, because I ain't going nowhere with you. Well, he wanted me bad, you know what I mean? So and so, well, they called the band to a meeting, and all the gang voted me in and voted this cat out. So he passed the rumor. The first time I find him playing somewhere, I'm going to go up there and run him out the joint. So we went on the road about three weeks after we gets a job at the Santa Center Club. And yeah, he walks in the door with his banjo. And when he walked in the door, he was playing a number. I'll never forget it. Think of me thinking of you. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. So when I seen him coming in the door, I made everybody get down with me in my rhythm. And I went to picking him. So, dun-dun-dun-dun-dun-dun-dun. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da 28 and I went with the tuxedo band but before I went with Sam Morgan I played with Willie Paggio too for nine months you see Danny Barker left here and went to New York and I took his place at this Jitney dance me him Wilhelmina Bork on the Nistropanion drums and a guy named Clarinet I believe his name is Joseph or something we used to call him Kaiser oh yeah yeah Kaiser Willie Joseph Willie Joseph we used to call him Kaiser play play clarinet and we had a real good band up there you know but that was a rough job the guy said don't let me hear the echo of the last piece die out before you pick up another one and that grind went on from nine to three and sometime my wrist I swear to God got as big as that rock from that constant playing and I mean but I was learning then you see because as I tell y'all learn plenty with John but what really made me a good enough fast reader was up there with Paggio because Paggio believed in his music him I don't care where he was at he wasn't no hell of a trumpet player but he knew what he was doing you see what I mean he was he was an excellent musician he read anything you put up there of course when you tell him the jazz now he was calling as a jazz man but as a musician he was tops I mean and he always believed in his music you know and he give everybody their part well reading all them pretty chords night after night and you're reading them from the orchestration and arranging and put them now if you was playing by ear you liable to just say make a flat C7 B flat C7 E flat C7 E flat C7 E flat the chord you but you're this card giving you G minor 7 B flat augmented night and all them beautiful and as you and that harmony is so rich and pure balancing against your ear that man you never heard nothing so beautiful in your life sometimes you could just feel your heart swelling in you the music was so pretty and beautiful you know what I mean so that's all I stood up there and I stood up there with him I said for about eight months and I played that stuff night after night after night after night well when I could go in any man's band and play that I didn't care what he put up there I'd play it you know

now did you ever have to substitute on any other instruments like what did you get one set off or a number off now and then so you could go and eat or anything well well no yes what no I had a racket it would cost me a nickel I'd break a straight take two hours to fix it that was the only racket I've heard sometimes like they take turns about to keep the drummer going all the time and one other guy would go and take the drummer's place and he could go out

well Bill I said this I love music and if I had my life to live over again I wouldn't be nothing else but a musician but not a badger player I'd be a trumpet player this time I better be you see cause everybody the bad you see I read in a little book kid Thomas with his enormous power he can play for 14 hours without stopping yeah but he don't play seven notes in them 14 hours either he said ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta Jackson and we had a Jackson Mississippi that wasn't, we had a real good band. But it didn't last too long. We went out on the road for a while. Must have lasted about eight or nine months. And conditions was bad on the road. So when I come back to Jackson, I got a very good friend in Jackson, Joe White. Fine drummer man off the Rabbit Foot Menstrual Show. Him and Manza Campbell supposed to be two of the greatest in the world. So he used to feature this number on the show called OU Drummer. And you never heard nobody play it like him and Manza Campbell. So I went on the show with him and after I played for old man Walcott, he said, well Joe, this man is everything you say he is with a banjo. But no man on my show plays one instrument. He must double on something else. So I had a friend from New Orleans was on the show, Skinny, played tuba. So he told me, say ain't nothing to it, Joe. He said, just get a horn and I'll show you your finger. So and so. Well, I took a peck horn. Well, I didn't like a peck horn. I'm all after. I didn't like that. So I fooled around, went in the back and I got me a trumpet. And I sat down and took my banjo and figured that trumpet out. And I joined that band. I was playing enough trumpet to hold myself up.

I was going to ask a little bit more. Wait a minute. Can you tell us a little about Wilhelmina Barth? Because I never did get to hear her. I know she was a good pianist. What style did she play? What kind of piano?

Well, like I told you, Bill, on a Jitney dance, you see the styles varied. When she came to work early at night, she might have played like pad of whiskey, like you say. But as the hours started to go, she was finally wide up playing like stormy weather, you know, just sitting up there caught in the wind. Because as I told you, the man used to wake us like mules. Don't let the echo of the first piece die out before you pick up another one. That was the rules we had. What size lady? Was she big and strong? Oh, yeah. She was kind of hefty. Yeah. She was kind of on the portly side. She was pretty strong. Had a heavy touch. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah. She had a very heavy hand. Yeah. She was a very good piano player. Did she teach music or read music and all of it? Well, yes. Yes. She read music. But as far as teaching it, I didn't know.
I heard that she's teaching now. Somebody talked like maybe she was teaching in late years.

Well, I wouldn't know. All I know is that she joined a church out there with another friend of mine. You remember that fellow I made you sell it right to Dr. Blanks? Oh, yeah. Yeah, well, she joined Dr. Blanks' church. That's on Bienville and Durban.
Does she live in town or across the lake or something?

Well, I don't know. I haven't seen her in quite a while. Last time I saw her when Percy's daughter. Percy's daughter got married. Oh, yeah. And we played up there that night, you see. And she was at the dance. I heard that too. Well, I haven't seen her since. Now, where she's at, I wouldn't know. But that's the last time I had an occasion to see her.
Okay, this just about finishes up. We can ask one more question about...
You asked something about Ernest Trepani, yeah?
Yeah, Ernest Trepani.
No finer drummer in the city than him at no time. A fine fellow and a fine musician at all times. Jovial, laughing all the time, and one of the finest timekeepers you ever sat next to. Yeah, yeah.
On parade...
Oh, he was the master of the parade. Of course, I never played with him on parade. But, I mean, all the other guys had the same acclamation as a parade man that I had for him as an orchestra man.
Was he a bass drum on parade?
Yeah, yeah. I used to play a bass.
Supposedly bass drum.
Yeah, uh-huh.
That just about ends up this side. This side will turn it over. Mm-hmm.
You were telling us about the band of the Alamo, who else was in there? Had the trombone player?

Oh yeah, the trombone player was Yank Johnson. Oh, he was very good. I mean, I kept having his name confused. I used to call him Yank Robinson all the time until I found out that he was Yank Johnson. Now here was a guy who played one of the sweetest trombones.
